title: Give me truth
hook: rather than love, money, fame, give me truth (Walden 18)
tomorrow: the sun is a morning star

segments.voice: Yesterday, a different drummer: the companion who falls behind, and Thoreau's generous perhaps. Who did you let walk at their own pace? Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

Love. Money. Fame. Set them on a table in front of a stranger and ask them to pick one, and you'd learn a lot about the stranger. A love song would pick the first. A business plan, the second. A talent show, the third. Thoreau, a few pages from the end of Walden, pushes all three aside and asks for something that doesn't fit on the table at all. It's one short sentence, and it's a strange order of priorities, because he puts love on the losing side. Today, what he asks for instead.
screen: `LOVE. MONEY. FAME.` → `PICK ONE.` → `THOREAU PUSHES ALL THREE AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, from Walden's Conclusion: "Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth." First, the shock of the list. Money and fame are easy to set aside in a book about a cabin. But love? He doesn't say love is bad. He says that if he had to choose, he'd take truth first, maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love. Second, a dinner. Right after this line, Thoreau tells of sitting at a table with rich food and plenty of wine and attentive service, where sincerity and truth were missing. And he says he went away hungry. A full plate, and he left hungry. That's how he measures a meal: not by what was served, but by whether anyone was honest at it. Third, what truth means to him here. A little earlier in the same chapter he writes, "Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe." Not what you ought to say. What you actually have to say. For Thoreau, truth isn't mainly a fact you look up. It's the difference between a real life and a performed one. Fourth, the cost. Choosing truth over love and money and fame means some rooms get colder. Some tables you leave early. Thoreau seems to accept that. He'd rather go home hungry than stay full on make-believe. Readers are free to argue with him. But the line is plain about where he stood.
screen: `TRUTH OVER LOVE, MONEY, FAME.` · `A RICH TABLE, AND HE LEFT HUNGRY.` · `SAY WHAT YOU HAVE TO SAY.` · then, large: `ANY TRUTH IS BETTER THAN MAKE-BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell the truth in one hard spot. Settle and breathe. Let one place come to mind where you say what you ought instead of what you have to say. A meeting. A family dinner. A friendship where something has gone unsaid. Don't rehearse a speech. Just find the one true sentence underneath, short and kind. Say it silently to yourself a few times, and notice how it sits. Then decide, gently, whether today is the day to say it out loud. The bell holds the time.
Give me truth. Thoreau's choice, ahead of love, money and fame, and his reason for leaving a rich table hungry. Today's word.
Your line: give me truth. Today, in one small place where you'd usually say the expected thing, say the true thing instead, kindly. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

screen: `DAY 1243 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUN IS A MORNING STAR.`

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often hold this line up as Thoreau's case for sincerity: saying what is actually so, even when the expected answer would be more comfortable.

fork.setup: you're at a table with rich food, fine wine and attentive service, but nobody is being sincere. what does Thoreau do?
fork.reveal: he says he went away hungry: a full plate, but no sincerity or truth at the table.

trapdoor: what you thought: give me truth means never tell a lie.
what it means: put a real life ahead of a performed one, even ahead of love, money and fame.

what a scholar hears: in Walden's Conclusion the line comes after the advice to say what you have to say, not what you ought, and just before the story of a rich, insincere table that left Thoreau hungry.

notes: Confirm exact wording against the 1854 text: 'Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth.' and 'Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe.'
Paraphrased, confirm: 'I sat at a table where were rich food and wine in abundance, and obsequious attendance, but sincerity and truth were not; and I went away hungry from the inhospitable board.'
'Maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love' is offered as an interpretation, hedged; a reviewer may cut it.
'Readers are free to argue with him' is the writer's framing, not a claim about reception.
Editor pass: fixed the order of the passage; in Walden the rich-table story comes right after 'give me truth', not before (teach and trapdoor).
